script.opening_words: There's a moment that happens to almost every person who tries to invest. It's usually around 11:00 p.m. on a Tuesday. You pull up your brokerage app for what feels like the hundredth time that month. You've been contributing $500, maybe a thousand, every month for years. You stare at the balance and something clicks and that something is usually is this even doing anything? If you've had that exact moment, you're not being paranoid. The math from where you're
script.ending_words: it for 20 years while it slowly, quietly, rudely refuses to show you what it's actually doing. Until one day, you check your account and realize you're not the same person you used to be. If this video helped it click for you, drop a comment telling me which level you're on right now. Hit subscribe for more breakdowns like this one, and I'll see you in the next one.
script.analysis: Full 16667 canonical characters read. A seven-level compound-interest narrative: 11 p.m. brokerage-app hook; premise ($500/month at 10%, Casey vs Jake); level 1 (year 1, $283 growth); level 2 discouragement (years 2-5), Jake cashes out, Dalbar gap; level 3 first crossover ($100K, Munger); level 4 snowball (year 15); level 5 acceleration (year 20, $104/day); level 6 inflection (year 25, Fidelity 50s comparison, Jake restarts); level 7 exponential (years 25-40, $3.16M, Buffett after 50); cost of waiting 10 years; reframe ("stay in your seat"); close. All balances reproduce under monthly compounding at 10%/12. Overstated: year-15 growth ($19,331 not ~$22,000), year-25 growth ($62,571 not ~$70,000). Inconsistent: Jake's $48,000 at 63 contradicts $300/month for 18 years (~$180,000). Fidelity $212,000/$77,000 not located. Nominal returns, no fees or taxes. The stored ending is complete.
beat_map: Level 2: discouragement; Jake cashes out; Dalbar.
Level 6: inflection, year 25; Fidelity comparison; Jake restarts.
Cost of waiting ten years; doubling runway.
